title: Equations of Lines and Planes in Space
short: Equations of Lines and Planes in Space
lead: A line in space is set by a point and a direction vector, a plane by a point and a normal vector. This section writes their equations, measures distances from a point to a line and to a plane, sorts pairs of lines into equal, parallel, intersecting and skew, and finds where planes meet and at what angle.
objectives: Write the vector, parametric, and symmetric equations of a line through a given point in a given direction, and a line through two given points.
Find the distance from a point to a given line.
Write the vector and scalar equations of a plane through a given point with a given normal.
Find the distance from a point to a given plane.
Find the angle between two planes.
summary_html:
• In three dimensions, the direction of a line is described by a direction vector. The vector equation of a line with direction vector $\kvecv=\langle a,b,c\rangle$ passing through point $P=(x_{0},y_{0},z_{0})$ is $\kvecr=\kvecr_{0}+t\kvecv,$ where $\kvecr_{0}=\langle x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}\rangle$ is the position vector of point $P.$ This equation can be rewritten to form the parametric equations of the line: $x=x_{0}+ta,$ $y=y_{0}+tb,$ and $z=z_{0}+tc.$ The line can also be described with the symmetric equations $\frac{x-x_{0}}{a}=\frac{y-y_{0}}{b}=\frac{z-z_{0}}{c}.$
  • Let $L$ be a line in space passing through point $P$ with direction vector $\kvecv.$ If $Q$ is any point not on $L,$ then the distance from $Q$ to $L$ is $d=\frac{\| \kPQ \;\times \;\kvecv\|}{\| \kvecv\|}.$
  • In three dimensions, two lines may be parallel but not equal, equal, intersecting, or skew.
  • Given a point $P$ and vector $\kvecn,$ the set of all points $Q$ satisfying equation $\kvecn\cdot \kPQ =0$ forms a plane. Equation $\kvecn\cdot \kPQ =0$ is known as the vector equation of a plane.
  • The scalar equation of a plane containing point $P=(x_{0},y_{0},z_{0})$ with normal vector $\kvecn=\langle a,b,c\rangle$ is $a(x-x_{0})+b(y-y_{0})+c(z-z_{0})=0.$ This equation can be expressed as $ax+by+cz+d=0,$ where $d=-ax_{0}-by_{0}-cz_{0}.$ This form of the equation is sometimes called the general form of the equation of a plane.
  • Suppose a plane with normal vector $\kvecn$ passes through point $Q.$ The distance $D$ from the plane to point $P$ not in the plane is given by $$D=\| {\text{proj}}_{\kvecn}\kQP\| =|{\text{comp}}_{\kvecn}\kQP|=\frac{|\kQP\cdot \kvecn |}{\| \kvecn\|}.$$
  • The normal vectors of parallel planes are parallel. When two planes intersect, they form a line.
  • The measure of the angle $\ktheta$ between two intersecting planes can be found using the equation: $\cos \ktheta =\frac{|\kvecn_{1}\cdot \kvecn_{2}|}{\| \kvecn_{1}\| \| \kvecn_{2}\|},$ where $\kvecn_{1}$ and $\kvecn_{2}$ are normal vectors to the planes.
  • The distance $D$ from point $(x_{0},y_{0},z_{0})$ to plane $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is given by $$D=\frac{|a(x_{0}-x_{1})+b(y_{0}-y_{1})+c(z_{0}-z_{1})|}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}=\frac{|ax_{0}+by_{0}+cz_{0}+d|}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}.$$

exercises.prompt: Find parametric and symmetric equations of the line passing through points $(1,-3,2)$ and $(5,-2,8).$

answer.solution: Possible set of parametric equations: $x=1+4t,y=-3+t,z=2+6t;$ related set of symmetric equations: $\frac{x-1}{4}=y+3=\frac{z-2}{6}$
answer.hint: Start by finding a vector parallel to the line.

exercises.prompt:

$$x=1-4t,y=3+t,z=8-6t$$ $$x=2+3s,y=2s,z=-1-3s.$$

answer.solution: These lines are skew because their direction vectors are not parallel and there is no point $(x,y,z)$ that lies on both lines.

Show that the line passing through points $P(3,1,0)$ and $Q(1,4,-3)$ is perpendicular to the line with equations $x=3+3t,y=1+8t,z=6t,$ $t\in \mathbb{R}.$

answer.solution: The line through $P$ and $Q$ has direction vector $\kPQ=\langle 1-3,4-1,-3-0\rangle=\langle -2,3,-3\rangle,$ and the other line has direction vector $\langle 3,8,6\rangle.$ Their dot product is $-6+24-18=0,$ so the directions are orthogonal. The second line passes through $(3,1,0)=P$ at $t=0,$ so the two lines meet at $P$ at a right angle: they are perpendicular.

exercises.prompt: Given point $P(1,2,3)$ and vector $\textbf{n}=\textbf{i}+\textbf{j},$ find point $Q$ on the x-axis such that $\kPQ$ and $\textbf{n}$ are orthogonal.
Show there is no plane perpendicular to $\textbf{n}=\textbf{i}+\textbf{j}$ that passes through points $P(1,2,3)$ and $Q(2,3,4).$

answer.solution: A plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$ has $\mathbf{n}$ as a normal vector, so every vector between two of its points is orthogonal to $\mathbf{n}.$ But $\kPQ=\langle 1,1,1\rangle$ and $\kPQ\cdot\mathbf{n}=1+1+0=2\ne 0.$ So $P$ and $Q$ cannot both lie in a plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}.$

exercises.prompt: Find parametric equations of the line passing through point $P(-2,1,3)$ that is perpendicular to the plane of equation $2x-3y+z=7.$
Show that line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-2}{4}$ is parallel to plane $x-2y+z=6.$

answer.solution: The line has direction vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle 2,3,4\rangle$ and the plane has normal vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 1,-2,1\rangle.$ Since $\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}=2-6+4=0,$ the line’s direction is orthogonal to the normal, so the line is parallel to the plane. (It does not lie in the plane: its point $(1,-1,2)$ gives $1+2+2=5\ne 6.$)

exercises.prompt:
Consider the planes of equations $x+y+z=1$ and $x+z=0.$

a. Show that the planes intersect.

b. Find symmetric equations of the line passing through point $P(1,4,6)$ that is parallel to the line of intersection of the planes.

answer.solution:
a. The normal vectors $\mathbf{n}_{1}=\langle 1,1,1\rangle$ and $\mathbf{n}_{2}=\langle 1,0,1\rangle$ are not scalar multiples of each other, so the planes are not parallel and therefore intersect; their line of intersection has direction $\mathbf{n}_{1}\times\mathbf{n}_{2}=\langle 1,0,-1\rangle.$

b. $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{z-6}{-1},\;y=4$
